items.title: Fostering vs. Adoption: Which is Right for Me?
items.snippet: Wondering whether fostering or adoption is right for you? In this podcast episode, Tim shares his experience of both and explores the key differences between the two. The post Fostering vs. Adoption: Which is Right for Me? appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
On the fence about whether you should foster or adopt?

In the latest episode of the Let’s Talk About Fostering podcast, host Faye sits down with Tim Jarvis, a bearded biker, former doorman, and business owner who has lived experience of both fostering and adoption.  

He and his wife Claire have been fostering for 14 years and currently have a teenager in their care, alongside raising their adopted daughter and biological son. Tim shares his insights into fostering, adoption, and what it’s like to be an unconventional foster parent.

What do Faye and Tim chat about?

Tim provides an honest account of what it’s like to foster vs. adopt and how they differ – from assessments and family time arrangements to life story work and support.   

If you’re ready to hear Tim’s take, tune in to him talking to Faye about: 

  • What inspired him and Claire to foster 
  • Fostering below the UK average age of 54 
  • What it’s like to be an unconventional foster parent 
  • The importance of diversity in fostering 
  • The dynamic between Tim and his foster daughter 
  • From only fostering teenagers to adopting the baby they fostered  
  • Tim’s advice on how to decide between fostering and adoption 
  • The key differences between fostering and adoption 
  • The truth about the fostering assessment  
  • The reality of adoption  
  • Helping a child understand their past 
  • Nurturing a sense of identity in foster kids 
  • Talking to birth children about adoption 
  • Quick fire questions  
  • Traits of a good foster parent  
  • Treating every child in the home the same 
  • Advice for prospective adopters and foster parents 
  • Who can foster 
  • Tim’s favourite moment so far 

“Anyone, anywhere can foster a child… and make an amazing difference.”

 

 Click here to watch – or search ‘Let’s Talk About Fostering’ on your chosen podcast platform.

Are you ready to make a difference?

If you’d like to learn more about fostering with FCA, call us today on 0800 023 4561 or submit your details via our online form. 

Whether you have specific questions or just want to find out more about the support, training, and allowances we offer here at FCA, our team are ready to help you.  

You can also discover what it’s really like to be a foster parent by listening to our other podcast episodes, reading our foster parent stories, and checking out our latest news and blogs.

Some young people begin life carrying burdens no child should ever have to face.

After arriving in the UK as a teenager, one young person had experienced unimaginable trauma and struggled deeply with their emotional wellbeing. Yet, despite everything, they showed incredible resilience.

With the consistent care, stability and nurturing support of a Compass foster parent they began to flourish. Sport became an important source of confidence, purpose and positivity, while hard work and determination helped them succeed academically too.

Today, that young person is thriving - pursuing higher education, developing their sporting talent and building a positive future for themselves.

Behind that success is a powerful reminder of what can happen when a young person is given safety, stability, encouragement and someone who believes in them.

Sometimes, a caring relationship really can change the course of a life.

And perhaps the most meaningful recognition came from the young person themselves:

“Thank you for always being amazing. You are the definition of a super mum. I am so proud to be your son, and I hope that you know that you have made my life much better and happier. I love you, Mum.”

Every young person deserves the chance to feel safe, supported and able to reach their potential. ❤️

items.title: Department for Education to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign
items.snippet: The Department for Education is launching a co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign in October 2026, due to a shortage of foster carers. The post Department for Education to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Department for Education to Launch Fostering Recruitment Campaign

The Department for Education (DfE) is launching its first fully co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign in October 2026, aimed at encouraging more people to consider fostering.

The heart of the campaign is not only the dispelling of myths and misconceptions around who can foster, but also about reframing fostering as an extension of who people already are, rather than asking them to become a different kind of person. Therefore, the campaign will highlight more of the everyday differences that people can make to children’s lives, over and above any perceived complex expectations or specialist skillsets that may feel out of reach.

The campaign has arrived at a time of decreased numbers of approved foster carers in the UK. According to the DfE, the number of foster carers has fallen by 12% since 2019, with research showing that misconceptions is a driving factor in people ruling themselves out before even exploring fostering.

TACT are passionate about dispelling fostering myths and misconceptions; the charity ran a campaign in September of 2025 called ‘Ordinary People Making an Extraordinary Difference’, which highlighted the everyday smaller gestures of care that can make a positive impact on young people. Another key message of the campaign was that fostering should be an option for people across all walks of life, and not just those with care-aligned vocational backgrounds.

TACT are proud to be supporting the upcoming co-ordinated fostering recruitment campaign, and look forward to engaging with each step as they are revealed by the Department for Education.

Read more about fostering myth busting on our Fostering Questions and Answers page.

items.title: Supporting Foster Children with Hidden Disabilities
items.snippet: Not all disabilities are visible. Foster children with hidden disabilities, such as ADHD, autism or FASD, may need additional understanding and support. Discover how hidden disabilities can affect everyday life and the practical ways foster parents can help children feel understood, supported and empowered. The post Supporting Foster Children with Hidden Disabilities appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
If you’re thinking about fostering children with disabilities, you might picture wheelchairs, hoists, and an adapted home.

While in some cases, this might be the reality when you foster a child with complex physical or medical needs, in others, they could have a hidden disability like ADHD, autism, or FASD, which means they require a different kind of support.

From what invisible disabilities look like and how common they are, to how they impact children’s lives and what you can do as a foster parent to support them, join us as we take a closer look at hidden disability foster care.

What is an invisible disability?

In the UK, around 70 to 80% of disabilities are ‘hidden’, meaning they aren’t immediately apparent to other people. Unlike some physical disabilities, which may be more visible, hidden disabilities, also known as non-visible or invisible, can often go unnoticed by others.

However, just because a disability or additional need isn’t immediately recognisable doesn’t mean it has any less of an impact on a person’s everyday life. From communication and behaviour to sensory processing and managing everyday situations, hidden disabilities can affect a child in several ways.

 

When people hear the words ‘invisible disability’, they might automatically think of conditions like ADHD or autism. While these are examples of ‘non-visible’ disabilities, there are many other conditions that fall under the ‘hidden’ umbrella, such as:

  • Mental health: Anxiety, depression, OCD, eating disorders, and PTSD.
  • Chronic illness: Diabetes, asthma, coeliac disease, and endometriosis.
  • Neurodiversity: ADHD, autism, FASD, dyslexia, dyspraxia, and dyscalculia.
  • Energy and pain: Chronic fatigue syndrome, chronic pain, migraines, and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes.
  • Cognitive: Brain injury, processing difficulties, and executive dysfunction.
  • Sensory: Hearing loss, tinnitus, sensory processing difficulties, and visual loss.

You can find a list of hidden disabilities and learn more about the challenges they can present on the Hidden Disabilities Sunflower website, an organisation founded to raise awareness of non-visible disabilities.

How to support a child with a hidden disability

At FCA, we’re here to help our foster parents feel confident and capable on your fostering journey. That’s why we’ve selected our top five tips for supporting children with hidden disabilities:

1. Understand the child’s condition

One of the best ways to support your foster child with their non-visible disability or additional need is to make sure you’re fully aware of what their condition is and how it impacts them as an individual.

Even if you know another child with the same diagnosis, it could present differently in your foster child. So do your research and pay attention to your young person to understand what individualised support they need.

At FCA, as part of our ongoing training, we offer specialised courses on topics such as ADHD, autism, FASD, and more, that give you the skills and knowledge to care for children with hidden disabilities.

2. Collaborate with professionals

When fostering disabled children, you aren’t expected to take on the role of their whole care team. You’ll work closely with relevant professionals to ensure your foster child’s needs are met and their entire well-being nurtured.

In addition to the help you’ll receive from your young person’s health care team, such as their GP, consultant, occupational therapists, or CAMHS, you’ll also have access to wraparound foster care support from us here at FCA.

Our Team Parenting Model includes input from therapists, social workers, education leads, participation officers, and other foster families, giving you even more people to lean on and learn from on your fostering journey.

3. Create safety and predictability

You and your home are your foster child’s safe place, and after a long day of managing their symptoms and, in some cases, masking, they need to feel able to relax and be themselves.

Make sure you have a predictable routine, with the same mealtimes and bedtimes so the child in your care knows what to expect, and that your home is adjusted to their needs.

For example, if you foster a child with sensory processing difficulties, you might have soft lighting, unscented products, and blackout curtains to prevent sensory overstimulation.

4. Always look beyond behaviour

For many children in care, their past experiences have taught them that expressing their thoughts, feelings, and needs is unsafe. As a result, they might struggle to tell you what’s going on in their inner world and whether they are finding things challenging.

This means they’ll often express themselves through their behaviour instead, and as their foster parent, you’ll need to work out what their actions are telling you.

For example, if your foster child has a meltdown every time you go to the supermarket, it could mean they find the environment overstimulating or triggering. You can then reach out to professionals in their care team and from FCA to support them more effectively going forward.

5. Celebrate their strengths

Your foster child’s hidden disability is part of who they are, but not all they are, so avoid letting it define them.

Focus on the small wins and what they can do, rather than centring everything around their condition. Encourage them to build connections with children who share similar struggles and enrol them in activities that they love.

This will help build their self-esteem and develop the independence they need for life after care.

Want to learn more about disability fostering?

If you want to make a difference in children’s lives by becoming a foster parent, call us today on 0800 098 4148 or submit your details via our online form to learn more about fostering children with disabilities.

From the fostering process, support, and training to fostering allowances and the benefits of choosing FCA, our friendly fostering advisors are ready to answer your questions and help you change young lives.

items.title: ‘Mr Gum’ Author Inspires Foster Children

items.content:
‘Mr Gum’ Author Inspires Foster Children

A famous author has inspired a group of TACT young people, in a workshop aimed at encouraging a passion for reading.

Andy Stanton, the celebrated author of the Mr Gum book series, led an online workshop organised by TACT Fostering – in line with their extensive year-long National Year of Reading campaign activities.

He took the participants through his own creative processes, including the time he wrote a story for his nephews on Christmas Eve (which they ignored as it was Christmas), only to find the story again years later ‘in a box’. That story became the first Mr Gum book.

No stranger to working with children, Andy said: “I’ve been talking to children in schools and at book festivals for twenty years now. I haven’t done any events or workshops for children in care before. Whomever I’m talking to I always strive to make my events inclusive and welcoming for all. 

“There’s a part of the workshop where I ask the children if they’ve ever woken up in the middle of the night with a crazy idea running through their head. I always love hearing the surprising answers that come out of that. Hopefully the children were engaged throughout, but these moments of interaction stand out [for me].”

Andy is also passionate about encouraging a love for reading in young people: “Reading can expand a young person’s horizons and make them aware that a whole world of opportunity is out there. Even if that opportunity is ‘just’ the opportunity to explore a different life or viewpoint for a while via escapist fiction – that’s invaluable and so many life lessons can be taught under cover of ‘only a story’!”

Tina Bull, an Education Advisory Teacher who works within TACT’s Education Service, echoed this sentiment: “Sessions like this, particularly when we can call on established writers and illustrators, are wonderfully inspiring for our young people.

“Throughout our sessions, if we can inspire just one of our young people to read more regularly or more widely, the work and planning for our year-long calendar of National Year of Reading activities will have been worth it.”

The National Year of Reading is a campaign aimed at bringing the joy back to reading for children and young people. It’s not an annual event. In fact, there have only been two other campaigns; in 1998 and 2008. In 2026, with smartphones and AI taking hold of our younger generations, the act of reading has taken a backseat. According to The National Literacy Trust, only 1 in 3 children and young people aged 3-18 currently enjoy reading in their free time, and only 1 in 5 read daily.

Research undertaken by the Department for Education has shown that children who are confident readers by the end of primary school can earn £65,000+ more over their lifetime compared to non-readers. The theme for the 2026 campaign is called ‘Go All In’, which encourages young people to read about their hobbies, interests and passions. This could include music, films, food and sport – using a wide range of different formats to make reading more culturally relevant, engaging and enjoyable.

items.title: What No One Tells You About Fostering – But Should
items.snippet: Fostering can be incredibly rewarding, but it also comes with challenges you might not expect. From emotional highs to difficult goodbyes, there’s plenty to learn along the way. Discover the realities of fostering and the things foster parents wish they had known before starting their journey. The post What No One Tells You About Fostering – But Should appeared first on Fosterplus.
items.content:
Fostering is one of the most rewarding careers that you can choose to do. Children in care often come, having experienced trauma, and need the love and support from a caring foster parent to heal and build brighter futures for themselves. Positive outcomes are only made possible because of the hard work of foster parents like yourself.

Although it’s a fulfilling role to explore, there are probably a couple of things that no one has told you about fostering – but should. We wanted to take a closer look at what these positives and negatives are, so that you can prepare yourself for all of the emotional highs and lows that fostering can bring.

So what does no one tell you about fostering, but you should know about?

Gratitude will be rarer than you think

When you start your fostering journey, you may have an idealised version of what it’s going to look like in your head. Lots of fun days out with your foster children, playing lots of games together at home in your free time, and your foster children being endlessly grateful for everything you do.

Sadly, you’re unlikely to get a thank you from your foster children for all of your hard work at the time. They may be appreciative of having somewhere safe and to be loved by you, but might not think to say ‘thank you’ to you directly.

A lot of our foster parents find that their grown-up foster children may get back in touch at a later date to show their appreciation when they’ve had time to reflect on all that you’ve done for them.

It’s okay to say no to a match

While you want to help as many children as you can, sometimes the best thing you can do for both yourself and the foster child is to say no to a match if it wouldn’t be a great fit. You should never feel pressured to say yes to a match if you don’t think it would be in the best interests of the child or your family.

The Fosterplus matching team work hard to make sure a match is right for everyone involved, and we’ll support you at each step of the way. If you need a break between placements to reset and recuperate, ready to go again in the near future, then it’s okay to say not now.

We believe that matching a child with the right foster family is crucial to a successful placement. A match has to be compatible for everyone before it can go ahead, so that everyone can have a positive experience.

Children will come with trauma

An important thing to note is that foster children are going to have experienced trauma, and it’s likely that, at times, that this trauma will display itself in how a child or young person presents. These children have lost the life they’ve always known, regardless of the circumstances, which can be very traumatic for them. Because of this, they’re likely to have behaviours that reflect that trauma.

At Fosterplus, all of our foster parents are trained to take a trauma-informed approach. We encourage our foster parents to look behind the behaviour to what it’s trying to communicate to you. We offer our foster parents training at each stage of their fostering journey, and tailor it to your needs and interests.

Training is split into:

  • Mandatory courses – every foster parent has to complete these with us, and they typically include topics such as safeguarding, first aid, and equality, diversity and inclusion among others.
  • Prepare to Foster – all of our foster parents have to complete this training, which gives you a basic and practical introduction to fostering.
  • Additional courses – alongside our Prepare to Foster and mandatory training, there’s a vast range of other additional training courses that you can complete. These vary depending on the topics, but include subjects such as Understanding Autism, Emotional Regulation, Foetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder and many more.

You get more support when you foster with an agency

You can choose to foster with your local authority or with an independent agency. While there are benefits to both, you’re more likely to get the proper support that you need if you choose to foster with an agency like Fosterplus.

Some of the support that you can look forward to with Fosterplus includes:

  • A dedicated supervising social worker with a realistic caseload
  • Competitive fostering allowances
  • A 24/7 helpline so you get support when you need it most
  • Training that’s tailored to your needs and interests
  • Regular support groups with like-minded foster parents
  • Expert matching

Celebrate those little things

While fostering can be challenging at times, there are always lovely moments that come alongside the more difficult ones, too. Nothing compares to seeing the unbridled joy on your foster child’s face when they experience something new for the first time, such as seeing the sea, going to the cinema, or visiting a new location on holiday.

Celebrate those quiet moments of joy and seeing the world through a child’s eyes once again. Moments like this can help us to better appreciate the things we have in life, and remind us not to take our privilege for granted.

It’s important to take care of your mental health

It’s so crucial to look after your mental health, especially when it comes to fostering. You’re only able to help the children in your care when you’re feeling at your best. So if you’re feeling less than 100%, it’s key to take some time out of the day to recharge those batteries so you’re ready to go again tomorrow.

You don’t have to dedicate hours to self-care to look after your mental health. It could be something as small as taking five minutes to unwind with a cup of tea, or going for a short walk around your local area. Spending time on a hobby, such as reading or a creative craft can help you to switch off, too.

Remember – self-care is never selfish.

Saying goodbye will be hard

The hardest part of fostering is often when you have to say goodbye to the young person in your care, whether that’s because they’re moving to a more permanent placement or they’re getting ready to start adult life outside of the care system.

It’s important to mentally prepare yourself for the day you have to say goodbye, and allow yourself the time to process your grief. Look at this as a positive for your foster child, and all the wonderful things that are to come for them because you gave them a safe space to grow.

This also doesn’t have to be a permanent goodbye, either. Many of our foster parents stay in touch with their foster children long after the placement ends. Consider exchanging details with your young person so that you can stay in touch, and make sure they know you’ll always be there if they need you.

Foster children become part of the family

One of the most beautiful things about fostering is that any young people you welcome into your home will become part of the extended family. If your foster child is staying with you as part of a long-term placement, then it’s only natural that they start to feel at home with every member of the family, including grandparents, aunts and uncles, and cousins.

As we’ve mentioned above, many of our foster parents stay in touch with their foster children once a placement ends. Some of these care-experienced adults choose to involve their former foster parents in their adult lives, too.

Becoming a foster family is one of the most rewarding things you can choose to do, both for yourself and the foster children you welcome into your home, as well as for your children and extended family.

You’ll still have meetings and paperwork

While fostering can be an excellent career choice if you want to avoid a job that means commuting every day, it’s worth noting that you’ll still have to deal with meetings and paperwork relevant to fostering. However, both of these are incredibly important when it comes to looking after the children in your care.

Meetings allow you the opportunity to advocate for your young person in a room of professionals. You can stand up for them and ensure that their needs are being met. While it might seem intimidating to be in a room with so many different people, don’t feel too scared to speak up and say your piece – you have just as much of a right to be there as anyone else.

There are lots of different types of paperwork that you’ll have to do, too, including:

  • Placement planning
  • Foster care agreement
  • Daily logs
  • Training records
  • Monthly progress reports
  • Annual reviews

Remember that the paperwork is actually there to help you, and to make sure that everything is documented properly.

Fostering is a commitment

Once you’ve welcomed a foster child into your home, it won’t simply be a case of taking them to school and sitting back and relaxing. It’s key to remember that fostering is a commitment, so you’ll need to think about whether short-term or long-term placements are better suited to your needs.

You’ll also need to balance the needs of your own children, if you have them, alongside those of the foster children in your care. Make sure that you explain to your children that foster siblings may need more attention and care at times, but that doesn’t mean you love them any less.

There are lots of different types of fostering for you to consider, depending on how much of a commitment you’re ready for.

An emotionally rewarding journey

Although fostering has its ups and downs along the way, there’s no doubt that this is one of the most emotionally rewarding journeys that you’ll ever experience. This is arguably one of the best benefits of fostering a child. Many of our foster parents remark on how uplifting it is to see how far their young people have come from the time that they first met them.

When a foster child comes to stay with you for the first time, they may be withdrawn and reluctant to trust those around them. It’s through your hard work that they’re able to build a bond with you, to heal from their trauma and grieve for what they’ve lost, and then look to the future. Seeing children hit those milestones that they may have missed because you were the one to give them the safe, loving home they needed will always be a special moment.

Want to know more about fostering?

Are you thinking about fostering but don’t know where to start? We’re here to help you make that all important first step on your fostering journey.

Simply fill out an enquiry form on our website or get in touch on 0800 098 4157 to speak to one of our friendly advisors. They can answer any questions you may have about fostering or discuss the process with you in more detail.

Every child deserves to have a loving home where they feel wanted and have the security and safety they need to live healthy, fulfilling lives. Could you be the person to make a difference in a child’s life?

items.title: Keeping Siblings Together in Foster Care: David & Sasha’s Story
items.snippet: David and Sasha began fostering after their children left home. Discover how they came to care for four siblings and the difference keeping them together has made. The post Keeping Siblings Together in Foster Care: David & Sasha’s Story appeared first on Foster Care Associates.
items.content:
Foster parents David and Sasha decided to start fostering once their own children had flown the nest.  

Over two years later, they are making an inspiring difference caring for four siblings. They share their exciting journey, the importance of keeping siblings together in foster care, and the real impact foster parents can have on a child’s life.   

 

Our plan to foster 

David and his wife Sasha had always planned to foster. For some foster parents, they choose to foster as a route to starting a family, some foster with children at home, and others wait until later in life – when they’ve retired or have an empty nest at home. There is no right time to foster, except when it feels right for you – and you feel you are ready to help make a difference to children’s lives.

David and Sasha shared their decision to foster and taking the first step:

“As a couple we always said one day when our own birth children reach adult life that we would look to foster. We initially enquired via our local authority but soon realised the support just wasn’t there. We heard about FCA after doing some deep diving online and the reviews we read were enough to help us make the initial enquiry.”

The couple are very passionate about fostering and their role in supporting children and young people.

“Having the ability to open our hearts and our home to children is a privilege to us. Being able to share a safe and secure environment and help shape a child’s future into something positive is one of the most rewarding things we can do at this point of our lives.”

The assessment process

To become a foster parent, families take part in a fostering assessment which involves a series of meetings with a social worker to discuss the fostering role and look at a family’s background and individual circumstances. The process ends with a panel meeting where a foster parent’s approval is finalised, and they are ready to start their exciting new journey.

David and Sasha enjoyed the fostering assessment process and have shared their experience of the process:

“We felt very welcomed by FCA from the first initial enquiry and very quickly we learned that we had picked the right IFA for us. Some people can find the process intrusive, but we actually really enjoyed it. We were open and honest about all aspects of our lives and so, when we were deep diving into our past, it was almost therapeutic as we talked about our own childhoods and reflected on areas that we hadn’t even realised shaped the people we are today.” 

The couple also shared their experience of the initial Prepare to Foster training at FCA:

“For us meeting ‘real foster parents’ during the training was the most significant as hearing experiences from real carers is so different to reading in text or watching a video, it’s very powerful and encouraged us even more that we were doing something that could change children’s lives.”

Caring for four siblings

Due to a severe shortage of foster families – and, in particular, those able to offer a home to more than one child – it is estimated that one in three children in care are separated from their brothers or sisters.

David and Sasha are very passionate about keeping siblings together in foster care, wherever it is possible, and welcomed four children into their family to ensure they could stay together.

“When we first passed panel, we were approved for up to 2 siblings, but we found ourselves initially with a sibling group of 3 who after a while became 4 due to a breakdown of a placement elsewhere.”

“Keeping these children together has been so important. The fact they are safe together gives them a feeling of familiarity which in turn gives them an added layer of security. Going into care is can be frightening, and if children can face this new scary chapter with a sibling by their side it can give them a lot of reassurance that they aren’t doing things alone.”

Are you thinking of fostering?

Download the FCA’s complete beginner’s guide to fostering a child. Find out more on how to foster a child and the process involved.

Download Guide

Life changing impact

Foster parents make such an incredible difference in the lives of children every day. For David and Sasha, the everyday family life they provide to their children is truly transformational. They said:

“Life is so busy, it can sometimes feel mad and chaotic, but our daily routines and boundaries always remain no matter what life throws at us in any given day. These rules and routines have given the children a strong sense of safety and stability and they have all flourished with the secure environment that surrounds their daily lives. We always say to other families to never underestimate how powerful daily routines are, we take them for granted but they are the foundation/starting blocks for children who have experienced trauma.”

“Other foster carers used to say to us, ‘are you mad having 4?!’ and now they say how lucky we are because the children are so happy and content. That’s all come from opening our hearts, our home and being consistent in everything we do, the children now feel safe, secure, loved and we encourage them all to be the best version of themselves.” 

The couple shared one of the moments where they realised they’d made a real difference in their foster children’s lives:

“We feel like we’re making a difference to our children almost daily to be honest. Every day is a new adventure with a new milestone. One of our placed children went from being a year behind the peers in her class to getting one of the highest SATS scores in her school within 12 months. There was no additional out of school tuition or anything like that, just a stable loving home and giving her the tools to help her reach her full potential. The children surprise us every day with how far they’ve come.”

“Thinking about the children who arrived with us, compared with the children we see before us today, can often bring a tear of joy and happiness.”

Support at FCA

When you foster a child, the support you receive from your fostering agency is crucial. David shared his experience of the support they have received.

“The support from FCA has been brilliant, we definitely feel part of a strong community, and the monthly support groups are an excellent way to spend a morning chatting to other carers and sharing experiences and knowledge. Our SSW is fantastic; she genuinely cares about our family unit and visits regularly. She is a great support and helps us advocate for the children in various areas of their lives.”

“One thing we didn’t realise about fostering is just what a great community of people you meet, people who open their home to others who need them.”

The couple have also benefitted from the extensive training and therapeutic courses provided at FCA.

“We have a huge amount of training available to us, both online and in person, and it’s really varied. Children are all unique and individual but there seems to be a training module for almost everything you can imagine, and it really helps you understand what the children are experiencing and gives us the tools to offer them the best support.”

Our advice

When David and Sasha began fostering in 2024, they knew they’d made the right decision and haven’t looked back.

“One thing we did differently to others is for the first 6 months we offered respite cover and support to other carers and this opened our eyes to lots of different children. In fact, it was taking care of a sibling group for a week that cemented our decision to focus on keeping a sibling group together and we haven’t looked back since.”

“Fostering has been one of the most rewarding experiences of our lives. If you want to make a positive change to a child’s life, there is no greater calling than to be a foster carer.” 

 

 

You don’t need experience to become a foster parent, just a passion for caring for children and wanting to make a difference.

items.title: A Summer Full of Fun in The North West
items.snippet: Our TACT North West team organised some fun and varied activities for our young people over the summer - with one young person completing an amazing personal challenge! The post A Summer Full of Fun in The North West appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
A Summer Full of Fun in The North West

TACT’s Fostering North West team were very busy over the summer holidays organising some brilliant activities for our young people. One of our young people even completed an amazing personal challenge!

We kicked off the summer with our Multi-Sports Activity Day, delivered by Sportibees. Following the success of this event last year, and after hearing so many positive comments from our children and foster carers, we were delighted to bring it back again. The day was packed with a variety of sports and activities, giving everyone the opportunity to get involved, try something new and have fun together!

Another one of our summer activities came directly from our young people, who asked if they could meet up for an escape room challenge. It was wonderful to see friendships that have developed over the years continue to grow and strengthen. Not only did everyone enjoy spending time together, but we’re pleased to report that all of our young people successfully escaped. A huge well done to them all!

Throughout the holidays, children and young people also enjoyed a range of other outings, including bowling trips, cinema visits, arcade afternoons and days out at local parks. These activities provided opportunities for fun, relaxation and they enjoyed spending quality time together.

We were also fortunate to join colleagues from TACT West Midlands and TACT East Midlands for the Children Who Foster Residential. This was a first for our two young people attending, making it an especially memorable occasion. They had the opportunity to meet and connect with other children who foster, building friendships and support networks that we hope will continue to grow long into the future. The residential was packed with exciting activities, including high ropes, bag jumps, zip lining and much more, creating experiences and memories that will last for years to come.

To round off the summer, we headed to Blackpool Pleasure Beach. Despite a few rainy spells, over sixty carers, young people and staff came together to enjoy a fantastic day of rides, laughter and fun. As well as being an opportunity for everyone to enjoy themselves, the day also provided a valuable chance for carers and children to meet new people, catch up with familiar faces and strengthen the sense of community that is so important across our service.

Alongside the group activities, we were also delighted to celebrate an individual achievement this summer. One of our young people took on the challenge of abseiling down Anfield Stadium. This was a remarkable accomplishment that required real bravery, and we are incredibly proud of them for embracing such an exciting opportunity.

We received some amazing feedback from our foster carers and young people:

  • “The boys always enjoy the activities and it was great to catch up with everyone!” – TACT Foster Carer
  • “When can we do another activity?” – TACT Young Person
  • “The older ones said they loved the big rides and were ‘made up’ to be big enough for the new ride! It was also perfect age-wise as there was something for all the kids so an all round perfect option for a day out” – TACT Foster Carer
  • “Thank you for the trip, we enjoyed it!” – TACT Young Person

A big thank you to our North West team for organising and facilitating these amazing activities for our young people!

items.content:
Want to know what it’s really like to foster very young children?

In this episode of the Let’s Talk About Fostering podcast, host Faye sits down with FCA foster mum Jamila, who began her journey 6 years ago after being inspired by her sister, who has fostered with FCA for 15 years.  

She currently cares for a 2- and 3-year-old sibling pair alongside a 5-month-old boy but has also cared for older children and has three teenagers of her own. 

Jamila and Faye explore the realities of fostering babies, including the joys of this type of fostering, how it differs from fostering older children, common misconceptions and how to prepare both practically and emotionally for their arrival and departure.  

What to expect from this month’s episode 

Jamila gets real with Faye about fostering babies, which at FCA typically means children between the ages of 0 and 3. 

So if you’ve ever been curious about becoming a foster parent to young children, sit down, relax, and listen to Faye and Jamila discuss: 

  • The difference between caring for younger and older children. 
  • Jamila’s favourite thing about caring for under 5s. 
  • The rewards of helping children feel safe enough to be themselves. 
  • The very real impact of trauma on young children. 
  • Misconceptions about fostering babies. 
  • Helping toddlers feel stable when welcoming a new child. 
  • How to practically, mentally, and emotionally prepare for a new foster child. 
  • Fostering babies on their own 
  • Challenges of fostering babies.  
  • Fostering babies alongside siblings 
  • A brief overview of parent and child fostering. 
  • Preparing and coping with saying goodbye to young children.  
  • Fostering siblings, and why it’s important to keep them together.  
  • Jamila’s favourite memory of fostering babies. 

“It’s being able to be part of pure innocence and joy from a little one. You can’t beat that feeling.“

 

 Click here to watch – or search ‘Let’s Talk About Fostering’ on your chosen podcast platform.

Learn more about fostering today 

If you’d like to make a real difference in the lives of children in care, whether they’re babies, toddlers or teenagers, call us today on 0800 023 4561 or submit your details via our online form.  

From fostering allowances, support and training to what to expect when you welcome your first child, our friendly advisors are ready to answer any burning questions you may have.

items.title: Making Memories at Llangrannog!
items.snippet: Our TACT Wales team organised and facilitated an exciting residential trip to Llangrannog for our young people! The post Making Memories at Llangrannog! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Making Memories at Llangrannog!

TACT’s Fostering Wales team took a group of young people on a residential trip to Llangrannog during the summer holidays – to try some new activities, spend some quality time together – and to create memories that will stay with them long into the future.

Eleven young people aged 8 to 13 attended from TACT, alongside nine children from our North Wales fostering partner, Foster Care Values (FCV). This was the first time FCV had taken their young people on a residential break, and it proved to be a very positive and successful experience.

From the very first evening, it was clear that friendships were beginning to form. The team-building activities helped everyone settle in, feel included and begin building trust with one another. Over the few days we were there, we could see confidence and independence growing in the young people. Some of the biggest highlights included walking down to the beach, splashing in the sea together (some fully dressed!) – and taking part in the tobogganing, which was fast, wet, exciting and full of laughter.

It was especially lovely to see so many of the young people try something new; they encouraged one another to step outside of their comfort zones by cheering each other on, and celebrating every achievement. Whether it was taking on a high jump onto a giant airbag or simply giving an unfamiliar activity a go, there were many proud moments and plenty of big smiles!

At the end of each busy day, it was just as meaningful to see everyone relax together; watching a film, eating popcorn, chatting about the day and sharing thoughts and life experiences in a calm and supportive space.

Feedback from our young people was wonderfully positive. Here are just a few of the comments we recieved:

  • “I have had fun with my friends and meeting new ones. I enjoyed getting splashed by the waves at the beach and feeling chilled there.”
  • “Llangrannog is the best place in Wales. I have already been here seven times with school and TACT. I love meeting friends.”
  • “You meet new friends for life. Go karting was my favourite activity.”
  • “I loved the experience. I had a great time, it was really fun and I made many friends that I’d love to see again.”

A big thank you to our Wales team for organising and facilitating such a wonderful trip for our young people!

items.content:
We’re celebrating 30 years of supporting foster families and helping children find safe, loving homes where they can thrive.

Over the past three decades, we’ve seen first-hand how fostering can transform lives.

Not through grand gestures, but through everyday moments. A warm welcome. A listening ear. A place at the dinner table. A bedroom a child can call their own.

As part of our 30th anniversary celebrations, we’re proud to launch two new films that shine a light on the incredible difference foster parents make and invite more people to consider whether they could do the same.

Because for many children, a spare bedroom is never just a spare bedroom.

It’s More Than a Room

Our new campaign film begins with a simple truth: “At first, it’s just a spare room.”

For many families, a spare room can become a home office, a guest room or simply a space that sits quietly unused. But for a child entering care, that same room can mean something entirely different.

It can be safety.

It can be stability.

It can be belonging.

It can be the first place they’ve ever truly felt at home.

The film explores how a bedroom can provide much more than four walls and a bed. It can offer comfort during difficult times, a sense of security, and the reassurance that someone is there to care.

After 30 years of supporting foster families, we know that fostering isn’t simply about having space in your home. It’s about creating space in your life for a child who needs it most.

Meet The Family Behind Our Campaign

Meet Allison, Ryan and Olivia and discover how two spare bedrooms became a place of safety, support and belonging. Watch their full story below.

Watch Their Full Story

Celebrating 30 Years of Support

As we celebrate our 30th anniversary, we’re reflecting on the thousands of children, foster parents, families and colleagues who have been part of Orange Grove’s journey.

For 30 years, we’ve had the privilege of supporting foster families through every stage of their fostering experience. We’ve witnessed children achieve milestones they never thought possible, and we’ve seen extraordinary foster parents help young people build confidence, resilience and brighter futures.

The need for foster parents remains as important today as it was 30 years ago. Every day, children and young people need safe, stable and nurturing homes where they can feel secure and supported.

Could Your Spare Room Change a Life?

Our campaign’s message is simple. If you have a spare room, you might already have the starting point for something truly life-changing.

You don’t need to be perfect. You don’t need previous parenting experience. What children need most is patience, understanding, commitment and the willingness to provide a safe place where they can belong.

As Allison says, fostering is about thinking about what you can do for a child. And as Ryan and Olivia’s story shows, that impact can last a lifetime.

As we mark 30 years of supporting foster families, we’re inviting more people to ask themselves one simple question: Could your spare room change a child’s life?

Ready to Learn More?

If you’ve been inspired by these stories and are wondering whether fostering could be right for you, we’d love to hear from you.

items.snippet: When Allison's daughter moved out, her home felt empty. With two spare bedrooms sitting unused, she never imagined they would go on to change children's lives forever. The post From Spare Room to Family appeared first on Orange Grove Foster Care.
items.content:
When her daughter moved out, Allison was left with two spare bedrooms. She never imagined they would one day change lives.

After being approved as a foster parent in March 2015, four siblings arrived at Allison’s door, including Ryan and Olivia, who were just seven and six years old.

“I was excited and terrified at the same time,” Allison laughs.

After being moved a number of times, he remembers arriving at a house he’d never seen before and meeting a woman he’d never met.

But what stood out immediately was the welcome. 

“She was very happy we were there. Very welcoming,” says Ryan. “There was a dog there too, Koda. That helped. It made everything feel more welcoming.”

Olivia remembers it much the same way. 

“I had the biggest grin on my face,” she says. “I remember walking in and giving Allison a hug. I remember the dog. I remember the spaghetti bolognese. It was the best meal I’d had in weeks.”

 

The Little Things That Make a Big Difference

For many children, a bedroom is just a bedroom. For Ryan and Olivia, it meant much more. Ryan remembers walking into a clean room for the first time. 

“There was a duvet cover on the bed. The sheets smelled nice. I had a wardrobe. I had carpet. It felt clean and welcoming.” 

Those details might sound small, but they left a lasting impression.

“The carpet felt soft under my feet,” he says. “It felt homely.” 

Olivia had a similar experience. 

“It was so clean,” she remembers. “The atmosphere was calm. Everything felt safe. I’d never really had that before.” 

For Allison, creating that environment was important from day one. 

“I wanted them to feel they were home,” she says. “That it was their room, their space, somewhere they could feel safe, loved and able to relax.” 

More Than a Roof Over Their Heads 

Over time, a house became a family home. Ryan has now lived with Allison for 11 years. He doesn’t call her Allison anymore. 

“I call her Mum,” he says. “I’ve lived with her longer than I lived with my biological mum. She is my mum.” 

Today, his bedroom is somewhere he can relax, spend time with friends and simply be himself. 

“It’s my place of security,” he explains. “It’s somewhere I can go if I’m upset. It’s my space.” 

Olivia feels the same. 

“My room is my happy place,” she says. “I can relax, read, study and spend time with friends. It’s somewhere I feel safe.”

But perhaps the biggest difference wasn’t the room itself. It was the relationships. 

“What makes a house a home is being able to come back and relax,” says Ryan. “To know you’re home.”

Growing Into Their Future 

Today, Ryan is 19 and preparing for a career in policing. He believes fostering changed the direction of his life. 

“My foster parent turned me into who I am today,” he says. “I’m kind. I’m on the right side of the law. I think I’ve turned out great.” 

Olivia, now 18, is studying A-levels and hopes to become a social worker so she can support other children who have experienced difficult beginnings. 

“I want to help children with similar stories to mine,” she says. 

Both young people talk openly about opportunities they never imagined they would have. And both are determined to give back. 

The Difference One Person Can Make 

When asked what fostering has given her, Allison doesn’t talk about awards or recognition. Instead, she talks about watching children grow. 

“Seeing them become young adults has been amazing,” she says. “To watch them achieve everything they have achieved makes me so proud.” 

Ryan agrees. Looking back, he describes meeting Allison as hitting the jackpot. 

“I feel very lucky,” he says. “I’m grateful every day that I stayed with Mum.”

And Olivia sums it up perhaps better than anyone. 

“When I was six, I thought nobody would ever really love me,” she says. “Now I feel so loved, and I’m so grateful for that.”  

Could Your Spare Room Change a Life?

For anyone considering fostering, Ryan has a simple message: 

“Be patient. Speak to children like actual people. Listen to them.” 

And Allison’s advice is equally straightforward: 

“Think about what you can do for a child. They need understanding, commitment, love and a safe place to call home.” 

Because sometimes, all it takes to change a life is a spare room, an open door and someone who cares.

Across the UK, so many children need the love, support, and care foster parents provide. If you believe you could be a good fit to foster, enquire with us today, or check out our blogs to hear from more foster parents just like Allison about what makes fostering such an amazing journey.

items.title: Without my foster parents, I’d probably be in jail” – a care leaver’s story
items.snippet: After experiencing abuse and neglect, Adam entered foster care at just four years old. Now 18, he reflects on how the support of his foster family helped him overcome challenges, find a sense of belonging, and build a more positive future than he ever thought possible. The post Without my foster parents, I’d probably be in jail” – a care leaver’s story appeared first on Fosterplus.
items.content:
Adam, 18, moved into his first foster home when he was just four years old, having experienced abuse and neglect at the hands of those he trusted most. Six years ago, he began living with the foster parents he now calls ‘Mum’ and ‘Dad’ and continues to stay in the family home while he waits for a space in supported accommodation.

Life hasn’t been easy for Adam, as he’s had to grapple with PTSD, bullying, and coming to terms with his experiences. However, with the support of his foster family, Fosterplus, and girlfriend, he has made big strides in his healing journey and feels like he ‘finally belongs’.

Adam believes his life would be very different if he hadn’t had his foster parents by his side and shared his story to encourage more people to consider fostering to give other children who’ve had similar experiences a ‘better chance of having a good life.’

The day Adam moved into care

The day a child moves into care, their whole world is turned upside down. They have to leave everything behind and walk into an uncertain future. Adam shared his experience of the day he was removed from an unsafe environment and entered care.

He said, “I can remember sitting in the HQ of a fostering agency in Birmingham, with so many people just staring at me. I was scared and confused – I don’t think I said a word to anyone.”

“I just felt anxiety and like I didn’t belong anywhere. I stayed at the HQ all night because they hadn’t found me a home. I moved in with a foster family the next morning with my brother.”

From uncertainty to belonging

Since that day, Adam has had three foster homes, finally feeling like he found his forever family when he moved in with his Fosterplus foster parents six years ago. They provided long-term foster care for Adam and encouraged him to stay put until he was ready to move on.

Adam said, “They make me feel like I finally belong. They’ve looked after me better than anyone else and have helped me find my own path.  I know they’ll always fight my corner if I need help.”

“I truly believe that if it weren’t for my foster parents, I would currently be in jail. But they fought so hard to keep me out of trouble and taught me how to stay safe.” 

“We’re like any other family, and I have a good relationship with their three sons, who’ve all left home. I have a 10-year-old foster sibling, too – we annoy each other, but we know we all love and care for one another, and that’s what matters most.”

Healing from trauma

The primary reasons children need foster care are abuse and neglect, which can have a lifelong impact on their well-being, affecting their behaviour, emotions, education, and relationships. Adam’s foster parents have helped him heal from his trauma and move forward. He is now studying construction at college and making big plans for his future.

Adam said, “My birth parents gave me severe PTSD and anger issues. I wasn’t just angry with them, but at the whole world. It was really hard at school. I was in fights most days and suspended most weeks. I had trouble studying, and only now has my brain finally caught up with everyone else who is the same age as me.” 

“But my foster parents have never given up on me, and it was their idea for me to stay at home until my supported living accommodation is ready, which has allowed me to go to college. They’re kind and understanding and won’t force or rush me into anything.”

“Eventually, I want to move to America, buy a piece of land, build my own house, and get married to my girlfriend. My foster parents have helped me get closer to my dream. They gave me a second chance at life, and I will always love them and be thankful for that” 

“They will always help you”

At Fosterplus, children in our care become part of our community – they are at the centre of everything we do. Adam has built strong bonds with his local Fosterplus team, knowing he can rely on them to support him with whatever he needs, whenever he needs it.

He said, “I don’t usually have favourites, but I do have two favourite members of staff at Fosterplus. They go out of their way to be there for me, and if I’m not at home when they do a surprise visit, they will always come back a few days later just to say hello to me.” 

“If I’m stressed, they know how to comfort me, and are always there to help a child in need. It doesn’t matter whether you’re a care leaver or still living in care. They will always help you.” 

Adam’s advice for anyone considering fostering

According to the Education Committee’s Social Care report 2024 – 25, 24% of the prison population have lived in care, and a quarter of those considered homeless are care leavers.

Adam is encouraging more people to become foster parents, to improve young people’s outcomes and help them live out their dreams. He shared his advice for prospective foster parents.

Adam said, “The kids will annoy you. They will push your buttons, stress you out, and make you go grey. I did it to my foster parents. But you need to remember that they’ve never had anyone who truly cares for them. You just have to give them time, and eventually they’ll grow out of it.”

“If you can support someone through their childhood and help them overcome all these really difficult things, you give them a better chance of having a good life and could stop them from getting arrested, ending up homeless, or going to prison.”

“You just need to have the right qualities – determination, resilience, and a strong will - because these kids will push your buttons. But overall, I think all you need is to be a good person.” 

Inspired by Adam’s story?

Adam’s story highlights the real difference foster parents can make in the lives of children and young people who’ve had a difficult start. When Adam’s foster parents welcomed him into their home, he found the family and sense of belonging that every child deserves.

If you’re over 21, have a spare bedroom, the legal right to work in the UK, and the desire to turn young lives around by becoming a foster parent, we’d love to hear from you. Call us on 0800 098 4152 or submit your details via our online form, and our experienced team will help you begin this life-changing journey.

items.title: Exciting Summer Activities in The West Midlands!
items.snippet: Our TACT West Midlands team organised some exciting summer activities for our young people! The post Exciting Summer Activities in The West Midlands! appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Exciting Summer Activities in The West Midlands!

TACT’s West Midlands team had a blast over the summer with our children, young people, and foster carers! We organised a variety of events which catered to different ages and interests and great fun was had by everyone!

We kicked things off at Cliff Lakes on 21st July. Cliff Lakes has a huge inflatable course on the edge of the lake, consisting of three sections for levels of ability. Seven of our young people attended this activity, and they were all competent swimmers. There were a lot of lifeguards present to ensure the safety of the children and they all wore wet suits and buoyancy aids.

Most of the children ended up in the third section of the course with more challenging activities which they thoroughly enjoyed. The session lasted for 90 minutes and we had lovely weather. There were friendships formed and everyone got along really well together, with some acts of kindness witnessed, helping and supporting each other.

After the session when everyone had changed into their dry clothes, we had lunch outside where the children chose their meals from the menu. A good day was had by all!

Next on the summer activity agenda was a painting activity in Walsall on 28th July, where the children copied a step-by-step painting from an artist. A silhouetted landscape of trees and animals was chosen. The children got to choose which animal they wanted to put in their painting, and we had a few interesting animals including Dinosaurs!

Eight of our young people attended, and the quality of the paintings produced was fantastic. The concentration and focus in the session was amazing, even for children who sometimes struggled with their concentration.

When we had finished our paintings, the artist gave the children sticky sparkles to add to their pictures. This went down really well and was a lovely way to finish the session. After the painting session we went to a Park and had a picnic for our lunch. The children enjoyed running around competing in races and playing tag, with the day ending with ice creams all round!

Our third activity was horse riding at Warren’s Hall Stables on 18th August. Six children took part in a range of activities, including grooming the horses, riding, and even enjoying a trot – which brought lots of smiles and a few giggles along the way!

The children were also involved in stable duties, helping to fill hay nets and muck out the horses. These hands-on activities gave them a greater understanding of how to care for horses and the responsibilities involved.

Being around horses can have a very positive impact on emotional wellbeing, and this was evident throughout the visit. The children appeared relaxed, engaged and confident during the sessions. All six children thoroughly enjoyed the experience and benefited from the opportunity to interact with the horses in a supportive and enjoyable environment.

A big thank you to our West Midlands team for organising such a range of activities, that balanced fun, creativity and education!

items.title: Report Highlights Need For Lifelong Support For Care-Experienced People
items.snippet: A report from the Department for Education has revealed shocking findings about mortality rates among care-experienced young people. The post Report Highlights Need For Lifelong Support For Care-Experienced People appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
Report Highlights Need For Lifelong Support For Care-Experienced People

Content warning: the following article and the report it links to covers sensitive and potentially distressing topics, including death, suicide, self-harm and the experiences of care-experienced young people who have come to harm. Please take care of your wellbeing and step away if needed. 

The Department for Education (DfE) has published an independent report highlighting shocking findings about mortality rates among care-experienced young people.

The report raised concerns about isolation, mental health challenges and a loss of support as young people transition into adulthood. 

Ashley John-Baptiste, who has spoken at several events organised by TACT Fostering, provided a Foreward for the report. He said: “It is a national tragedy that so many care-experienced young people are dying so early in life and that, resultantly, a report like this is required.

“I have substantial lived experience of the care system. Yet despite this, nothing could have prepared me for the heartbreaking stories we have encountered. These young lives ended far too soon.”

Key findings from the report highlight that in 2025 the DfE received 112 notifications of deaths of care leavers in England, age 18 to 24 – three to four times higher than within the general population. Of those, 42% were female and 58% were male. More death notifications were recorded for care leavers aged 18, compared to all other ages in the 18 to 24-year-old range, with one fifth occurring at age 18.

These concerns have aligned with many aspects TACT has long campaigned for, such as smoother transitions into adulthood and greater investment in the relationships that matter most to children and young people. This is why TACT established their Connect community, providing their care-experienced young people with support into adulthood and beyond.

The challenges many care-experienced people face do not simply disappear when they reach a certain age. Strong relationships, a sense of belonging and access to support remain important throughout adult life, and TACT believe that care-experience should never mean facing adulthood alone.  

As reforms in children’s social care continue to develop, lifelong support must remain a priority. Connect is one example of how this can be achieved in practice: creating lasting relationships, strengthening communities and ensuring support is available whenever its needed.

items.title: Why it’s Okay to Say No to a Match
items.snippet: Finding the right fostering match is essential for both children and foster carers. While it can be difficult to turn down a potential placement, saying no when a match doesn’t feel right can lead to better outcomes for everyone involved and help create more stable, successful fostering experiences. The post Why it’s Okay to Say No to a Match appeared first on Fosterplus.
items.content:
Our referrals team work hard to find the right matches for foster parents like yourself and the foster children in your care. We want to make sure that everyone can have a positive fostering experience, and that this is the right place for a child to thrive.

It can be hard to turn down a match if something doesn’t feel right for you and your family. But it’s crucial that you only say yes to a match that you know will be suitable for everyone involved, whether that’s interim foster care or a more long-term placement.

We’re going to explore why it’s okay to say no to a match, and why this could be the best outcome for you and the foster child in some cases.

Safe, compatible matches

The most important thing that our referrals team look at when it comes to pairing foster parents with children is whether this is a safe, compatible match for everyone involved. There’s no science to matching – our referrals team go into a lot of detail to make sure that the match is the best one for all of you.

Considerations

While it’s good to keep an open mind when it comes to considering a match, it’s best to think about what you can offer the foster children that would come to stay with you. What do you feel you’d be able to accommodate in terms of additional needs? Is there any training we can offer you to improve your skillset?

Compatibility

Another crucial factor to matching is the compatibility between yourselves as foster parents and the children you welcome into your care. If the foster child needs a lot of one-to-one attention, but you already have a foster child and birth children at home, then it’s not likely to be a good fit.

Our foster parents often refer to this as the ‘magic of matching’. There are so many different factors that come into play to make the right match, and it’s so important that everything is right so that this match can go ahead. It’s a careful, evidence-based process that we take pride in getting right.

Saying ‘yes’ to the wrong match

We know it’s hard to say no to a child in need. However, if you don’t feel that you’d be able to support that child’s needs, or there are extenuating factors that could have a negative impact on others in the home, then it’s important that you say no to the foster placement.

That’s because the last thing we want for both you and the child who could be placed in your care is a placement breakdown if things don’t work out. This can be detrimental to everyone involved. You might feel like you’ve failed – which wouldn’t be the case at all; it just wasn’t the right match for either of you.

All of our foster children, their needs and welfare, are our priority at Fosterplus.

Foster children and placement breakdowns

Any placement breakdown could cause further trauma to a foster child, and affect them in multiple ways. ‘Giving it a go’ just because you feel bad about saying ‘no’ to a match that isn’t quite right could do them more harm than good.

Here are a few ways that a foster child could be affected:

  • Re-traumatisation – the breakdown in your relationship with a foster child could re-traumatise them all over again, especially if they’ve had multiple placements.
  • Attachment issues – a foster child may struggle to form attachment with other carers in the future, as they might feel that this next placement won’t last long, either.
  • Mental health – this could have a profound impact on their mental health and make them question their self-worth.
  • Behaviours – big emotions could come into play more often if a foster child has experienced a placement breakdown.
  • Trust – a foster child may struggle to trust other adults in the future.

When to turn down a foster placement

You shouldn’t feel guilty at saying ‘no’ to a match if it doesn’t feel right, or now isn’t the right time. There could be any number of reasons that the match doesn’t seem like a good fit. Here are a few examples of when it’s okay to say ‘no’ to a match:

  • Age constraints – if the proposed match is with a child that’s outside of the age range that you feel able to support, such as a young toddler if you’re used to caring for teenagers, it’s okay so stick to what you feel comfortable with.
  • Safety concerns – if there’s a safety risk to your own children, other foster children already in the home, or vulnerable family members.
  • A mismatch of needs – perhaps the foster child has a range of complex needs that don’t match your expertise. While we do offer a wide variety of training courses, some of the more specialised areas may require someone with knowledge and experience in that field, such as mother and baby foster placements.
  • Disrupting household dynamics – if you feel adding a child into your home could have a detrimental impact on the children already in the home.
  • Burnout and capacity – it’s okay to say no for now if you need some time in between placements so that you can recoup your energy and mental capacity to help those in need.

The importance of good matching in fostering

We pride ourselves on our specialism when it comes to matching. Our referrals team is unrivalled in their attention to detail, ensuring that both our foster parents and the children in their care are able to have a positive fostering experience.

The right match can change lives. Here’s why a good match can be so important for children in need:

  • Sense of belonging – a good match can give foster children a sense of belonging with their new foster family. Quite often foster children will stay in touch with their foster family once a placement ends, and become part of the family.
  • Stable, secure base – giving children a place of safety where they can just be children allows them to enjoy a childhood.
  • Love – each and every child deserves to be loved. The right match will give a child the love that they need to thrive, and have a positive impact on their sense of wellbeing.
  • Easier transitions – minimising the disruptions that children have to experience is important for their wellbeing. A good match will ensure that a foster child doesn’t have to experience this and they’re better able to transition to the next stage of their life.
  • Positive outcomes – giving children the security they need to move past their trauma is essential. With the right match, a child can flourish and build a positive, brighter future for themselves.

Preventing placement breakdowns

The last thing anyone wants is a placement breakdown. Without the right support, foster parents can feel isolated or burnout, and might not be able to deliver the care that foster children need. That’s one of the many reasons why we’re so passionate about giving our foster parents the support they need, when they need it most.

Wrap-around support

When you foster with Fosterplus, you’ll get support at each stage of your fostering journey. We offer our foster parents:

  • Access to 24/7 support.
  • A dedicated supervising social worker.
  • Training tailored to your needs and interests.
  • Regular support groups to meet likeminded foster parents near you.
  • Expert matching.
  • Events and activities for all the family.
  • Specialist support from an Education Advisor, therapeutic services, and more.
  • Free membership to FosterTalk.

Trauma-informed care

Sadly, children in care are going to come with trauma. Around 60% of children who come into care do so because of abuse and neglect. Other children may have lost a parent or grandparent. They might be part of a large sibling group that weren’t able to stay together.

It’s important to take a trauma-informed approach and to look beyond the behaviour to the child underneath. Trauma can present itself in a variety of ways, so we ensure that our foster parents receive trauma-informed training to give them the tools they need to help the children in their care.

Short break care

Fostering can be a hard job, so sometimes you might need to take a break to reset and come back refreshed and better able to deal with its challenges. We offer our foster parents up to two weeks of paid respite leave if they need it.

Transparent matching

To be able to deliver the best care for a child, you need to know all about them before they come to stay with you. Transparent matching works in everyone’s best interests, as once you know a child’s needs upfront, then you’ll know how best to help them.

Throughout the matching process, you’re able to ask any questions that you may have about a match before it goes ahead. Social workers can also ask to know more about you and your experience, too.

 

Start your fostering journey today

Are you curious about fostering and matching? Start your fostering journey today with Fosterplus. From short-term and respite care to long-term fostering solutions, there are so many different ways to open your heart and home to children in need.

If you want to know more about the application process, fill out an enquiry form on our website or give us a call on 0800 369 8512 to speak to a friendly member of the team who can discuss fostering in more detail.

A Fantastic Summer Event

Here are some of the comments received during the day –

“Our young person has made lots of friends and really enjoyed it”.

“The climbing wall was brilliant”.

Bringing our Fostering Community Together

We had a fantastic turn out for this event, from across the regions, and we got to see a lot of happy faces – children and foster parents too.

Events like these are such a wonderful opportunity for our foster parents and children to meet with others who understand fostering, enjoy time together and build life-long friendships.

As well as creating plenty of memories, our wonderful foster families also helped raise £71 for Cancer Research UK through the tombola. A huge thank you to everyone who contributed and helped make the day such a success!

items.title: TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care
items.snippet: TACT have joined forces with The Fostering Network to lobby the Department for Education for free school meals for children-in-care. The post TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care appeared first on TACT.
items.content:
TACT Lobby For Free School Meals For Children-In-Care

TACT have joined forces with The Fostering Network to lobby the Department for Education (DfE) to extend free school meals entitlement to all children in foster care.

In June 2025, the government announced that, from the 2026 to 2027 academic year, the eligibility criteria for free school meals in England would be expanded to all children in households receiving Universal Credit. Whilst this was a welcomed decision for those households, a significant number of young people in foster care would not be eligible for those free school meals.

TACT immediately joined forces with The Fostering Network and approached the Department for Education (DfE). They agreed to co-design a survey that The Fostering Network would share with all members. The survey closed on Sunday 9th August and it had a huge response, with 713 foster carers in England completing the survey, highlighting the importance of this issue.

There were some significant key findings.

51% of foster carers stated that the children they foster are expected to lose their free school meal entitlement from September 2026, despite living in low-income households – as carers are unable to claim Universal Credit due to savings exceeding eligibility thresholds, often set aside for retirement or used to meet the needs of children in their care. The survey also found that household incomes were only slightly above the eligibility threshold, and that some were ineligible for Universal Credit due to being above State Pension age.

A number of foster carers highlighted significant financial concerns, with many estimating that the loss of free school meals would increase costs by more than £100 per child per month. This was a particular concern for foster carers with 3+ children all currently on free school meals. With fostering allowances not universally increasing to offset these costs, carers reported that they may need to reduce spending on other essentials, including clothing and/or activities for children.

There was strong support for automatic free school meals entitlement for all children-in-care, regardless of their foster carer’s income or benefit status. Many carers reported that free school meals provided continuity, stability and routine for children. This was seen as particularly important during transitions, such as moving between foster families or reunification with birth families. Many also cited the local authority’s role as corporate parent, arguing that children-in-care should automatically qualify for free school meals.

Foster carers also expressed considerable concerns about the wider implications of losing free school meals entitlement, particularly the potential loss of access to the Holiday Activities and Food (HAF) programme. As HAF eligibility is linked to benefits-related free school meals, children-in-care who lose their entitlement may also lose access to holiday activities, food provision and opportunities for social engagement.

The survey results are now with the DfE and TACT are lobbying them to extend free school meals entitlement to all children in foster care.
